questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Different culture, nature and architecture to Denmark. I wanted to choose a study destination which was known for good weather and that was a safe travel destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It wasn't that easy. Even though I got help from the host institution, a lot of information was (both for good and bad) left unexplained to find out for one self. Overall, I was able to finde the information I needed without too much strain and effort.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was welcomed by the host instituion and their abroad group. They were very helpful in a lot of ways. However, I didn't need most of the information that they provided.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The host institution provided us with external websites and off-campus oppurtunities. They were pretty expensive, but also very luxurious. There's many ways to find off-campus options on your own with facebook pages, whats-app and others.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In general, it's more expensive than living at campus. However, depending on where the uni is located, and how big the city you're staying at is, off-campus housing lets you choose where in the city you want to live and how close to the center (and campus) you want to be. For many cities, the central part is the heart of the city where the night life is booming and it's easier to meet and make friends. It's generally also where the most attractions are found.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to formally apply and choose the courses I wanted from a list I had already made. Then, I had to set up a user for their website and other platforms (which was pretty easy). All in all, the process is easy to follow and doesn't take long.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There were people to talk to, chat bots and phone numbers you could call to get help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful with all courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Understand that this instituion (by deafult) relies on a good reputation and therefore demand a lot from their students. Meaning, there's many assignments during semester (which often aren't coordinated well with other units, especially for exchange students), teachers would like students to be active and do their pre-reading before class. However, it's not as bad as it sounds. Exams are often off-campus and without supervision, meaning you can sit at home and not have to feel like you're being watched whilst doing your exams. Most lectures are done via Zoom and recorded so you don't have to be there every time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I chose three courses for third year bachelor's and one for second year. The one's that were for third year were, of course, more hard than the one for second year.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was very different. There's many assignments during the semester which also count towards the final grade. In-person classes are very active and often have some sort of experimental case or topic of debate around it. Lectures were recorded and could be watched at home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: BIO2040 - Conservation Biology, BIO3132 - Biology of Australian Vertebrates, BIO3070 - Advanced Ecology and Evolution, BIO3052 - Animal Behavior.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
"BIO3052 - Animal Behavior" was an excellent course which is well-praised for its excellent teaching method with weekly meetings with a mentor for a project and a seminar afterwards (the seminars are even recorded and can be seen at home). The project you're doing is very interesting and fun, and you get to meet new people and try and make your own experiment. Your mentors are very good at making sure everyone is doing their job and not leaving anyone behind. The exam is off-campus and is very short. If you listen in on the seminars and note down the important stuff from them, you're pretty much guaranteed to pass.

"BIO3132 - Biology of Australian Vertebrates" was amazing by having multiple field studies and case studies where the student is forced to think for themself and be more independent. There's a lot of work during the semester, but it's so worth it. Many of the assignments are even based on forms and reports that many students that graduate will do in the future. You also learn all about the amazing fauna of Australia and some of its history. The exam is also off-campus and short. And it only counts for 30% of the final grade. So, if you get good grades on your assignments, you won't even have to pass nor attend the exam technically.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food can be very expensive (unless you make it yourself, then it's mostly cheaper than DK prices). Travelling is very expensive. Transportation is expensive in the long run.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation, processed foods, housing.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were many different groups and classes to attend in your spare time. They had a whole sports centre for people interested in sports. There were also many oppurtunities to speak with christian mentors and other religious people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I very much enjoyed badminton as I did in my youth. Many people from Australia, specifically in Melbourne, are from Asia. They're very good and super friendly.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go on hikes around Melbourne. The hills and mountains around the city are sublime, absolutely astonishing. The Great Ocean Road is definitely a must see. Go visit at least one sanctuary in the city, and visit the Melbourne Zoo and Sea Life. Also, there's an 11h ferry to Tasmania from Melbourne which is delightful. Another must see is the east coast. Even if you don't like beaches or sunbathing, the east coast is so big and diverse that you're bound to find something that's to your liking.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It took some time, but I pretty much adjusted to it after 2 weeks.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to different social clubs, attend classes at uni, go out and party, message people in the city on Facebook or Whats-app to plan travelling with other people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Some people in classes stick to a clique and don't really let anyone else in. This can be hard as an exchange student. Most people need to have a full-time job to afford rent and living expenses so it can be hard to plan with Aussies.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They're very friendly by saying hello and waving when walking by or shopping/going on a reastaurant. Many non-Aussies are welcomed with open arms. Australia is indeed a multicultural country.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Work load is hard and a lot more than DK
2. Socialising can be hard, especially as an exchange student. Make sure you attend some social club or other do some other form of socialization at least once or twice per week.
3. Don't let the size of Australia scare you. Start small, explore your own city first and then venture out to see the beauty that is Australia.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Money are expendable, don't hog on money and spend as little as possible every day (unless you're broke). Studying abroad is a once in a lifetime oppurtunity that should be expensive, but also filled with memories, adventures, friends and fun. You can always earn more money when you're back, or you can extend your stay and work there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Travelling. Going out and exploring and taking in some of the breath taking scenic views of Autralia is so worth it. Even going a few hours to another city provides you with such a different experience than the last one. Australia is so big that there's something for everyone. You can even go skiing in the "cold" winter months.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Dealing with being on your own and not having your family around or anyone else can be very stressful and hard to deal with. It makes you tough and more independent. It provides you with valuable experiences that forces you to get out of your comfort zone and get out of bed. For me, this is the greatest challenge, but also a neccesity which many people lack in this modern world.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
